day-28-act-01.title: Descriptive statistics: mean, spread, and honest summaries
day-28-act-01.prerequisites: Day 27 mathematics block; basic arithmetic and the prediction-review routine from Day 01.
day-28-act-01.objective: Compute and interpret mean, median, population/sample variance, and standard deviation on a small dataset, and explain why two datasets with the same mean can still differ.
day-28-act-01.assistance_policy_label: Assistance allowed only after prediction and observed evidence are recorded.
day-28-act-01.instructions: Statistics begins by compressing data into a few numbers. The mean locates the center; variance and standard deviation measure spread around it. Population variance divides the squared deviations by n; sample variance divides by n−1 (Bessel's correction) to avoid systematically underestimating spread. Predict every value by hand before checking with `python3` — verification comes only after recorded predictions.
day-28-act-01.exercise_prompt: For data = [2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9]: compute the mean, median, sum of squared deviations, population variance, population standard deviation, and sample variance (divisor n−1). Then compute the mean and population standard deviation of data2 = [4, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 6] and state what stays the same and what changes.
day-28-act-01.hint: Mean = 40/8 = 5. Deviations: −3, −1, −1, −1, 0, 0, 2, 4. Squares: 9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16 → sum 32. Population variance divides by 8; sample variance by 7. For data2 the mean is also 5 but the squared deviations sum to 2.
day-28-act-01.answer: mean = 5.0, median = (4+5)/2 = 4.5, Σ(x−μ)² = 32, population variance = 32/8 = 4.0, population std = 2.0; sample variance = 32/7 ≈ 4.571 (sample std ≈ 2.138). data2 shares the mean 5.0 but has SS = 2, population variance 0.25, std 0.5 — the mean alone hides the spread.
day-28-act-01.mastery_criterion: All hand-computed values match a Python check, and the explanation states that equal means do not imply equal distributions.

day-28-act-02.title: Sampling uncertainty and the standard error
day-28-act-02.prerequisites: Activity 28-01 complete; no AI assistance for this practice block.
day-28-act-02.objective: Quantify how much a sample statistic moves: the standard error of the mean σ/√n and of a proportion √(p(1−p)/n).
day-28-act-02.instructions: In statistics, a sample mean is itself a random variable: repeat the sampling and it changes. Its standard deviation — the standard error — shrinks like 1/√n, so quadrupling n halves the error. Work the items by hand first, then verify with `python3 -c` one-liners using math.sqrt and math.comb.
day-28-act-02.exercise_prompt: (a) With σ = 2, compute SE(mean) for n = 16 and n = 64. (b) For a fair-coin proportion, compute SE(p̂) = √(0.25/n) for n = 4, n = 100, n = 400. (c) Using math.comb, compute P(X ≥ 7 heads in 10 fair flips) = [C(10,7)+C(10,8)+C(10,9)+C(10,10)]/2¹⁰ and state whether 7 heads is strong evidence of a biased coin.
day-28-act-02.answer: (a) SE = 0.5 (n=16), 0.25 (n=64). (b) 0.25, 0.05, 0.025 — the error halves each time n quadruples. (c) P(X≥7) = 176/1024 ≈ 0.1719 — about one fair coin in six does this, so 7/10 heads is a toy observation, not a statistical claim of bias.
day-28-act-02.mastery_criterion: Both SE formulas applied correctly, the √n halving pattern stated, and the binomial tail computed and interpreted without assistance.

day-28-act-03.title: Inference versus a single observation
day-28-act-03.prerequisites: Activity 28-02 complete; record your prediction before asking for help.
day-28-act-03.objective: Distinguish a statistical claim (a statement about a population with quantified uncertainty) from a toy observation (one small-sample result), and construct a misleading single-result counterexample.
day-28-act-03.assistance_policy_label: Assistance allowed only after prediction and observed evidence are recorded.
day-28-act-03.instructions: Inferential statistics attaches uncertainty to a claim: an estimate plus a standard error or interval. A single result is not a claim. Compare two toy models on 20 held-out examples: model A scores 16/20, model B 18/20. Before concluding B is better, ask how often equal-skill models would differ this much — each model's proportion has SE √(p(1−p)/20) ≈ 0.089 at p = .8 and ≈ 0.067 at p = .9 - in count units the SD is √(20p(1−p)) ≈ 1.79 at p = .8, 1.34 at .9 - so under a stated independence assumption a ±2-count gap is within ordinary fluctuation; the shared held-out set leaves A/B covariance unspecified, so this is not a paired or significance test.
day-28-act-03.exercise_prompt: Construct the counterexample: two learners each flip a fair coin 10 times; A gets 4 heads, B gets 7. (a) What are p̂_A and p̂_B? (b) Using Activity 28-02's SE for n = 10 (≈0.16), would you claim B's coin is biased? (c) Write one sentence separating the observation from a statistical claim.
day-28-act-03.hint: Compute each p̂, each SE √(p̂(1−p̂)/10), then the SE of the difference ≈ √2·0.16 ≈ 0.22. The observed 0.3 gap is about 1.3 standard errors — ordinary noise.
day-28-act-03.answer: p̂_A = 0.4, p̂_B = 0.7; SE(p̂) ≈ 0.158 per coin, SE of the difference ≈ 0.22; the 0.3 gap is ≈1.3 SE — inside ordinary fluctuation, so no bias claim is licensed. Observation: 'B's coin landed heads 7 of 10 times.' Statistical claim: 'at this n, a fair coin produces ≥7 heads ≈17% of the time, so the data do not establish bias.'
day-28-act-03.mastery_criterion: Learner produces both p̂ values, the SE comparison, and an explicit sentence distinguishing observation from claim; no fabricated significance is asserted.

day-28-act-04.title: Retrieval and statistics review checkpoint
day-28-act-04.prerequisites: Activities 28-01 through 28-03; use recovery link day-25 if earlier probability is shaky, and revisit Activities 28-01..03 for this day's statistics material.
day-28-act-04.objective: Close the block with closed-book retrieval: define the statistics vocabulary, compute a fresh summary unaided, and name what evidence turns an observation into a claim.
day-28-act-04.instructions: Without notes or AI: define mean, median, variance (population vs sample), standard deviation, standard error, and baseline. Then compute the full summary of data3 = [1, 3, 3, 5]. Finally answer: which two quantities must accompany any generalization beyond a toy observation? Use recovery link day-25 for missed probability basics, revisit Activities 28-01 through 28-03 for statistics misses, and record a review plan.
day-28-act-04.exercise_prompt: data3 = [1, 3, 3, 5]: compute mean, median, Σ(x−μ)², population variance and std, sample variance and std. Then solve for the n that makes SE(p̂) = 0.05 for a fair-coin proportion (solve √(0.25/n) = 0.05).
day-28-act-04.hint: Mean 3; deviations −2, 0, 0, 2 → SS = 8. Median = 3. Solve 0.25/n = 0.0025 → n = 100.
day-28-act-04.answer: mean = 3.0, median = 3.0, SS = 8, population variance = 2.0, std = √2 ≈ 1.414; sample variance = 8/3 ≈ 2.667, std ≈ 1.633. √(0.25/n) = 0.05 → n = 100. A claim needs an estimate plus quantified uncertainty (an SE or interval) and a sample large enough to bound the noise.
day-28-act-04.mastery_criterion: Unaided answers are numerically correct, all six vocabulary terms are defined from memory, and a concrete review plan names any term that was missed.
